title: Overhead Allocation: Getting Shared Costs onto the Right Line
summary: Overhead allocation decides which product or service carries which shared cost. Learn the main methods and how a weak allocation base distorts margins.
body_markdown:
## What Overhead Allocation Is and Why the Method Matters


Overhead allocation is the reason two capable leaders can read the same accurate P&L and disagree about which product is worth selling. It’s the method a business uses to spread shared costs that no single product, service, job, or customer caused onto the lines that actually consumed them. Done one way, your custom work looks like the premium end of the business. Done another way, the same custom work loses money on every order.


Reallocation never changes total company profit by a dollar. It only changes which line the profit shows up on.


Every cost falls into one of two buckets. Direct costs trace to one output without an assumption. Overhead, also called indirect cost, is everything else, and getting it onto a product or service line requires a choice. Overhead allocation is that choice, written down and applied the same way every period.


The line between direct and overhead isn’t a matter of taste, and federal tax law draws it explicitly. The uniform capitalization rules at[26 CFR 1.263A-1](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/26/1.263A-1) define indirect costs as all costs other than direct material and direct labor costs, and require a taxpayer to “make a reasonable allocation of indirect costs between production, resale, and other activities.” Two things follow for an owner. If the business carries inventory, it is already allocating overhead whether or not anyone decided to. And the standard is reasonableness, not one prescribed formula.


Financial reporting draws the line the same way.[FASB Statement No. 151, Inventory Costs](https://storage.fasb.org/fas151.pdf) requires fixed production overhead to be allocated to conversion costs based on normal capacity of the facilities, not on whatever happened to get produced in the period. Unallocated fixed overhead from a slow quarter becomes a current-period charge instead of being buried in inventory value.


In federal contracting, where allocation gets audited rather than assumed,[48 CFR 9904.418-40](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-48/chapter-99/subchapter-B/part-9904/section-9904.418-40) states the test in plain language. Indirect costs have to sit in pools that are homogeneous, and pooled costs have to be allocated “in reasonable proportion to the beneficial or causal relationship of the pooled costs to cost objectives.” Those cost principles do not bind a private commercial business. They’re still the clearest published model of what a reasonable allocation means, and that phrase reframes the question for any owner. The question is never what base is standard in your industry. It’s what actually makes the cost go up.


The arithmetic itself is one division and one multiplication. Pool divided by total base units gives a rate, and the rate times a line’s base units gives that line’s share. Nobody gets that part wrong. What goes wrong is the upstream choice of what sits in the pool and what the base measures, and a business can run correct arithmetic all year while pointing leadership at exactly the wrong product.


Three nearby questions sit outside this page. Reading margin by customer, product, and segment to decide what to grow or fix is covered in our guide to[profitability analysis and margin improvement](https://www.indinero.com/blog/profitability-analysis-margin-improvement/) . Building a per-location P&L and deciding how much corporate cost each site carries is multi-location profitability work. Splitting a period-over-period margin change into price, volume, and mix is a separate exercise again.


## How a Crude Allocation Base Distorts Product and Service Margins


A crude allocation base doesn’t spread overhead evenly. It hands overhead to whichever line consumes the most of that one base, which is how a high-volume simple product ends up paying for the complexity of a low-volume custom one. The subsidy is invisible on the P&L because total profit is correct.


Only the line-level numbers lie.


### What a plantwide rate does to a two-line manufacturer


Take a specialty manufacturer at roughly $8M in revenue, one company-wide overhead pool of $2,400,000, and a base of 60,000 direct labor hours. The plantwide rate is $40 per direct labor hour.


Standard line Custom line


Units per year 48,000 2,000


Direct labor hours each 1.0 6.0


Total base hours 48,000 12,000


Overhead allocated $1,920,000 $480,000


Overhead per unit $40 $240


The standard line absorbs 80 percent of all overhead for exactly one reason. It consumes 80 percent of the labor hours.


Now split that same $2,400,000 into five homogeneous pools, each with a base that reflects what drives it.


Cost pool Amount Driver Standard Custom Rate


Machine setup $600,000 setups 100 500 $1,000 per setup


Purchasing and expediting $480,000 purchase orders 2,000 6,000 $60 per PO


Engineering change orders $420,000 change orders 200 1,000 $350 per order


Machine running cost $540,000 machine hours 24,000 3,000 $20 per hour


Facility and plant admin $360,000 direct labor hours 48,000 12,000 $6 per hour


The standard line now absorbs $1,058,000, about $22 per unit. The custom line absorbs $1,342,000, or $671 per unit. That means $862,000 of overhead moved from the standard line to the custom line, and the total is still $2,400,000. Not one dollar of cost was added, removed, or reduced. Company profit is identical under both methods.


Per unit Standard, plantwide Standard, activity view Custom, plantwide Custom, activity view


Price $110 $110 $1,500 $1,500


Direct cost $62 $62 $900 $900


Overhead $40 $22 $240 $671


Margin $8 $26 $360 loss of $71


Under the plantwide rate the custom line looked like the premium business and the standard line looked like a commodity grind. Leadership would reasonably push sales toward custom work. Every custom order won makes the company slightly worse off, and the standard line keeps paying for it. The pattern is well documented in open-access teaching material:[Saylor’s managerial accounting text](https://saylordotorg.github.io/text_managerial-accounting/s07-03-using-activity-based-costing-t.html) runs a boat manufacturer at a $32 plantwide rate and shows a deluxe model earning $850 per unit turn into a $530 loss per unit once activity drivers are applied, while the basic model improves. When that margin ranking feeds the[KPI dashboard leadership steers by](https://www.indinero.com/blog/kpi-dashboards-for-business-leaders/) , the error travels into every decision made from it.


### The distortion each common allocation base introduces


Every pool needs a cost allocation base, the measure you divide the pool by. Each of the five common ones is defensible for the pool it causally relates to and indefensible for the rest.


- **Direct labor hours.** Still the most common base and increasingly the least defensible. It assumes overhead rises with human time, so when setup, procurement, engineering, and inspection are the real cost drivers, it routes overhead to whichever line has the most hands on it.
- **Machine hours.** Honest for depreciation, power, maintenance, and tooling. Dishonest for anything administrative. A machine-hour base on a pool holding the purchasing department punishes long production runs and rewards complexity.
- **Revenue or sales dollars.** The most common mid-market default and the hardest to defend, because revenue is a result, not a resource. A line pays more for being large rather than for consuming anything, and allocated cost moves when price moves, which makes year-over-year comparison meaningless.
- **Headcount.** Reasonable for HR, payroll processing, benefits, and recruiting, which genuinely scale with people. Unreasonable for facility and equipment cost. A ten-person line in 500 square feet shouldn’t carry the same rent as a ten-person line occupying half the building.
- **Square footage.** Reasonable for rent, property insurance, janitorial, and building utilities. Unreasonable for everything else, and it under-charges office-based lines that consume disproportionate management attention.


Pool homogeneity is what makes a base honest. One pool holding rent, the purchasing team, machine depreciation, and the CEO’s salary has no honest base at all, because those four costs are driven by four different things.


### Why it stays hidden


The distortion conceals itself for three reasons. Total profit is right, so the audit and the tax return are fine. The absorbed total always equals the pool, so everything foots. And the direction of the error is consistent, so a bad margin ranking looks stable year over year and gains credibility through repetition. The people who notice first are usually in operations, and what they say is some version of “that can’t be right, the custom jobs tie up the whole shop.” They’re describing a cost the allocation never charged them for. A margin report can be internally consistent, tie cleanly to the general ledger, and still be wrong about which product is worth selling.


## The Main Overhead Allocation Methods and When Each Fits


There are three practical overhead allocation methods, and they differ in exactly one way. How many cost pools they use. One pool for everything is a plantwide rate, one pool per department is departmental rates, and one pool per activity is activity-based costing. More pools buy more accuracy and cost more to maintain every month, so if you want to know how to allocate overhead costs in a way that survives past year two, choose the cheapest method that still produces a margin ranking leadership would act on.


Most published material on activity based costing for small business and mid-sized companies treats the full activity model as the destination. It skips the step most of these businesses should actually take first.


### A single plantwide rate


One pool, one base, one rate. It’s the least accurate method and the least expensive to run, and it’s the right answer more often than accounting purists admit. A business with a narrow set of similar outputs that consume shared resources in roughly the same proportions gains nothing from more pools. If every job runs the same steps in the same sequence with the same setup burden, a single rate isn’t a shortcut, it’s correct, and adding pools would add monthly cost without changing a single decision. The method breaks the moment output diversity appears. It assumes all overhead is driven by one factor, so it fails when one department’s cost follows machines and another’s follows labor, or when the business sells both a high-volume standard item and a low-volume engineered one. That second configuration is extremely common in a $5M to $15M manufacturer or project shop.


### Departmental rates


One pool per department or cost center, each with its own base chosen to fit that department. This is the plantwide approach with the pool count raised to match the organization chart, and it’s the highest-return, lowest-cost move available to most businesses this size. It requires no new data capture. The business already knows which department owns which cost and already tracks hours by department for payroll. What it fixes is the single largest source of distortion, which is a base that fits one part of the business and not another. For a company with three to eight recognizable functional areas and meaningfully different cost structures across them, departmental rates typically close most of the gap to a full activity model at a fraction of the monthly burden. What they don’t fix is complexity inside a department. If the setup crew spends ten times as long preparing the custom line, a departmental labor-hour rate still averages that away.


### Activity-based drivers


One pool per activity, each with a driver that measures consumption of that activity. In a mid-market business the usual set is setup driven by number of setups, procurement by purchase orders, engineering by change orders, quality by inspection hours, order management by order lines, shipping by shipments, and customer service by tickets. Three conditions make it worth the maintenance, and a business should meet at least two. Overhead is a large share of total cost. The mix is genuinely diverse in how it consumes support resources, usually a long tail of low-volume, high-touch work alongside a high-volume core. And a real decision is waiting on the answer, such as repricing a customer tier or deciding whether to keep a line, which is where[pricing strategy and financial discipline](https://www.indinero.com/blog/pricing-strategy-financial-discipline/) picks up. This method fails on maintenance far more often than on logic. Driver counts have to be captured every period or the model goes stale and quietly reverts to a labor-hour rate with extra steps.


### Fitting the method to the business


Business shape Method that fits


Few similar outputs, similar resource consumption, low overhead share Plantwide rate


Recognizable functional areas with different cost structures, some machine-driven and some labor-driven Departmental rates


Diverse mix with a low-volume high-touch tail, overhead a large share of cost, a live pricing or keep-or-kill decision Activity drivers on three to five pools, departmental or surrogate rates on the rest


This isn’t a maturity ladder to climb. It’s a cost-benefit test, run once a year. And the honest version for a 30-person company is not fifteen activity pools. It’s three to five pools covering the activities where the business is genuinely different from itself, plus one residual pool on a sensible surrogate base. A hybrid isn’t a compromise. For an established business it’s the normal end state, and the design work behind it is what[indinero CFO Services](https://www.indinero.com/services/cfo-services/) does with owners facing this question.


## What a Defensible Allocation Approach Looks Like


A defensible overhead allocation isn’t the most detailed one available. It’s one that passes four tests. Each pool is homogeneous, each base has a causal relationship to its pool, the method is written down and applied consistently, and moving to a more detailed method wouldn’t materially change the answer.


### The materiality screen that tells you when to stop


The federal cost standards supply the test that stops endless refinement, and it’s the step most allocation projects skip. A pool counts as homogeneous if each significant activity in it has a similar beneficial or causal relationship to cost objectives, or if allocating the pool as a whole produces a result that is not materially different from allocating each activity separately. Run that screen before you build anything. Take the pool in question, allocate it both ways on one period of real data, and compare the answers. If the ranking barely moves, stop. The simpler method is the correct one, and the business just avoided a recurring monthly burden it would have resented by March. This is why so many of these projects get abandoned in year two. Nobody ever decided how much detail was enough.


### Two anchors worth checking yourself against


Private-company overhead rates vary too much by industry for a single benchmark to mean much. The federal cost principles do supply two anchors that work as sanity checks, and they’re useful precisely because somebody had to defend them.


Under[2 CFR 200.414](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-2/subtitle-A/chapter-II/part-200/subpart-E/subject-group-ECFRd93f2a98b1f6455/section-200.414) , an organization without a negotiated federal indirect cost rate may elect a de minimis rate of up to 15 percent of modified total direct costs, raised from 10 percent effective October 1, 2024. No private commercial business is required to follow that figure. It is, though, the government’s current working assumption about reasonable administrative indirect cost for an organization it hasn’t audited, and a general and administrative burden running at multiples of it is something worth being able to explain.


The second anchor is what the base excludes. Modified total direct cost means direct salaries and wages, applicable fringe benefits, materials and supplies, services, travel, and up to the first $50,000 of each subaward. Capital expenditures, equipment, and the portion of large pass-through contracts above $50,000 are deliberately kept out, because leaving them in lets one capital purchase or one big subcontract swallow a disproportionate share of overhead and distort every other line. Mid-market businesses make exactly that mistake when large pass-through material and subcontract costs sit inside a revenue or total-cost base.


For inventory businesses there’s a third anchor, and it isn’t optional. The normal-capacity requirement means fixed production overhead is allocated on expected normal production including planned maintenance downtime, and the per-unit fixed overhead charge doesn’t rise because of an abnormally slow quarter. A plant that normally runs near 80 percent of capacity and drops to 40 percent books the overhead attached to that unused capacity as a period expense, not as inventory value. Because that same allocation reaches the tax return through the uniform capitalization rules, loop in the team handling your[business tax filings](https://www.indinero.com/services/business-tax-services/) before changing a method mid-year.


### Writing the method down, and the signals it has stopped working


The written policy should be short. What sits in each pool, the base for each pool and the causal reason it was chosen, the source system each base is measured from and who owns that data, whether rates are predetermined or actual and how absorption variances get cleared, the review cadence, and the materiality result that justified the pool count. Rates get recalculated annually during budget. Pool structure gets revisited whenever the business changes shape, meaning a new facility, a new product family, a significant equipment purchase, or a step change in headcount.


Watch for these:


- Margins by product or service line rank in an order nobody in operations believes.
- The rate still runs on a base chosen before a significant change in equipment, mix, or headcount.
- One pool holds costs driven by obviously different things, like rent, procurement labor, and machine depreciation.
- Price increases produce smaller margin gains than expected, the signature of a revenue-based allocation.
- Custom, rush, or small-batch work shows margins at or above standard work.
- Large absorption variances appear monthly and get written off without anyone asking why.


Consistency is the defense. Change the method at a clean period boundary, restate the prior period on the new basis, and keep both views for one cycle so leadership can see what moved.

## Frequently asked questions


Owners and leadership teams tend to arrive at overhead allocation with the same handful of questions, usually after a margin report stopped matching what operations was seeing. Here are the ones that come up most.


### What counts as overhead and what should sit in direct cost instead?


Overhead is any cost that can’t be traced to one output without an assumption, and direct cost is everything that traces cleanly. Federal tax law draws the same line, defining indirect costs as everything other than direct material and direct labor. So a business carrying inventory is already allocating overhead whether anyone decided to or not. Indinero CFO Services sets where that line sits and why, and indinero accounting codes the books to match.


### What is an allocation base and how do you choose the right one?


An allocation base is the measure you divide a cost pool by, and the right one is whatever makes that pool’s cost go up. Direct labor hours, machine hours, revenue, headcount, and square footage are the common ones, each defensible only for the pool it causally relates to. Revenue is the weakest default, since a line then pays more for being large rather than for consuming anything. Indinero CFO Services picks and documents the causal reason for each base.


### When is activity-based costing worth the extra effort for a growing business?


Activity-based costing earns its keep when overhead is a large share of cost, the mix is genuinely diverse, and a real decision is waiting. Meet at least two of those three and the maintenance is usually justified. For a growing business, departmental rates usually come first, since they need no new data capture and close most of the gap at far lower monthly burden. Three to five activity pools plus one residual pool is the normal end state.


### How often should a business revisit the way it allocates shared costs?


Recalculate overhead rates annually during budget, and revisit the pool structure whenever the business changes shape. Changing shape means a new facility, a new product family, a significant equipment purchase, or a step change in headcount. Make the change at a clean period boundary, restate the prior period on the new basis, and keep both views for one cycle. Indinero CFO Services sets that cadence with owners and documents the reason behind each change.


### Can a poor allocation make a profitable product look like a loser?


Yes, a poor allocation base can make a profitable product look like a loser, and a loss-making line look premium. A plantwide rate on direct labor hours routes overhead to whichever line has the most hands on it, so a high-volume simple product subsidizes a low-volume custom one. The distortion hides because total profit stays correct and everything foots. Operations usually spots it first, saying the custom jobs tie up the whole shop.


### Does changing the allocation method change the total profit a business reports?


No, reallocation moves profit between product and service lines without changing the total profit a company reports. Splitting one pool into five with better bases can shift hundreds of thousands of overhead dollars between lines while the pool total stays identical. The one exception is timing for inventory businesses, where the allocation affects what gets capitalized into inventory versus expensed in the period. What changes is which part of the business looks worth growing.
